name: Shan (Tai Yai)
variety: Shan of Shan State, Myanmar (Tai Long, also called Tai Yai), as written in the modern Shan script: five tones plus a sixth, emphatic tone
sources: Edmondson, Jerold A. (2008). Shan and other Northern Tier Southeast Tai languages of Myanmar and China: themes and variations. In Anthony V. N. Diller, Jerold A. Edmondson & Yongxian Luo (eds.), The Tai-Kadai Languages. Routledge.
Sao Tern Moeng (1995). Shan-English Dictionary. Dunwoody Press.
Glick, Irving I. & Sao Tern Moeng (1991). Shan for English Speakers. Dunwoody Press.
Cushing, Josiah Nelson (1887). Grammar of the Shan Language, 2nd edition. Rangoon: American Baptist Mission Press.
contrasts: aspirated against unaspirated stops (p pʰ, t tʰ, k kʰ); no voiced stops, unlike Thai and Lao
five tones, with a sixth used for emphasis (a regular lexical tone in northern dialects)
vowel length only in the low vowel, a against aː, in closed syllables and diphthongs
back unrounded ɯ ɤ against back rounded u o
final stops p t k against final nasals m n ŋ
the diphthong aɯ, kept apart from ai
allophony: f is [pʰ] in most dialects; [f] is used in eastern dialects and in loanwords
r occurs only in loanwords (Pali, Burmese, English) and is often replaced by l or h
final p t k are unreleased
a syllable written with an initial vowel begins with a glottal stop
the falling tone 5 ends in a weak glottal closure
syllable_structure: C(w)V(ː)(C) plus tone; the coda is one of p t k m n ŋ or an offglide i, u, ɯ
phonotactics: no initial clusters except a consonant plus w
codas are limited to p t k m n ŋ and offglides
checked syllables (ending in p t k) carry fewer tones than open and nasal syllables

stress.rule: Not described in the sources used; as in related Tai languages the last syllable of a compound or phrase is the most prominent.

rhythm.notes: No instrumental rhythm study of Shan is known to the compiler; low confidence.

length.notes: Only a and aː contrast in length; no measured ratio is known to the compiler.

intonation.declarative: lexical tones are kept; final particles carry much of the sentence-type meaning
intonation.yes_no_question: marked by a final question particle; no instrumental description of the melody is known to the compiler
intonation.accent_shape: no pitch accents; the sixth, emphatic tone (343) is used on a word to express emphasis or strong feeling
intonation.notes: Shan intonation is essentially undocumented; entries are general and of low confidence.

tone.confidence_notes: The five-tone system and the approximate shapes are standard in descriptions and teaching materials of Shan State Shan; the Chao digits are those usually quoted and are also the ones written in the comments of eSpeak NG's ph_shan. Dialects differ, and no instrumental F0 study is known to the compiler.

inventory.name: tone 3, mid, slightly falling (written with the mark ႈ)
inventory.description: Mid level, falling a little at the end.

inventory.name: tone 5, falling, creaky (written with the mark ႉ)
inventory.description: Short, strongly falling, with creaky voice and a weak final glottal closure.
inventory.phonation: creaky, with a lax final glottal stop

inventory.name: tone 6, emphatic (written with the mark ႊ)
inventory.description: Starts at mid, rises a little and drops at the end. Used for emphasis in most of Shan State; a regular lexical tone in northern dialects.

tone.notes: No tone sandhi is described in the sources used. Checked syllables are reported to contrast high, low, mid-falling and falling-creaky tones. No absolute F0 values are given here.

phonation: creaky voice and weak glottal closure on tone 5
no phonation contrast in consonants; aspiration only

problems: the tokenizer ends the word at the tone marks U+1087 to U+108A and at the asat U+103A, so the whole-syllable entries of shn_list and the context rules of shn_rules cannot match: ၵႃႇ, ၵႃႈ, ၵႃႉ and ၵႃႊ are all spoken with tone 1, and only the mark း (tone 4) is applied; in running text the marks for tones 2, 3, 5 and 6 have no effect
for the same reason closed syllables written with the inherent vowel lose it: ၶဝ်ႈ comes out as [kʰw], ၼမ်ႉ as [nm], ၽၵ်း as [pʰk]
the rules give the short vowel signs i and u a fixed tone 5, so ၵိၼ် is spoken with the falling tone instead of the rising tone
when the mark း ends up as a separate token it is read out by name, as 'Myanmar letter' followed by the digits of its code point (1038)
no sentence intonation and no declination: CalcPitches_Tone() in src/libespeak-ng/intonation.c ignores the clause type, and a question gives the same audio as a statement
the tonal pitch range is very small: pitch values 10 to 50 give about 78 to 97 Hz at the default voice pitch (under 4 semitones)
tone 5 has no creaky voice, no glottal closure and is not short
the aspirated t (t_h) uses the recording of plain t; ph_shan marks this as still to be done
the back unrounded vowels are rendered as central vowels: ɯ as [ɨ] (phoneme i.) and ɤ with the formants of a central rounded vowel (phoneme W, file vowel/8_2)
long aː is only a quarter longer than short a (250 against 200) and has the same quality
good: the six tone phonemes have the shapes given in the literature (rise 20 to 40, level 10, fall 30 to 20, level 50, fall 40 to 20, rise-fall 30 to 40 on eSpeak's pitch scale)
Shan is flagged as a tone language, so tone phonemes set the pitch of each syllable
aspirated and unaspirated p and k use separate recordings
the diphthong inventory, including aɯ, and the Shan digits and number words are present

notes: The status of the voice in eSpeak NG is 'testing'. The Thai voice inherits this phoneme table unchanged.
